In [[mathematics]], '''probabilistic metric spaces''' are a generalization of [[metric space]]s where the [[distance]] no longer takes values in the non-negative [[real numbers]] {{math|'''R'''<sub>{{space|hair}}≥{{space|hair}}0</sub>}}, but in distribution functions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sherwood |first=H. |date=1971 |title=Complete probabilistic metric spaces |journal=Zeitschrift für Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und Verwandte Gebiete |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=117–128 |doi=10.1007/bf00536289 |issn=0044-3719|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Let ''D+'' be the set of all [[Cumulative distribution function|probability distribution function]]s ''F'' such that ''F''(0) = 0 (''F'' is a nondecreasing, left [[continuous mapping]] from '''R''' into [0,&thinsp;1] such that [[Maximum|max]](''F'') = 1).

Then given a [[empty set|non-empty]] set ''S'' and a function ''F'': ''S'' × ''S'' → ''D+'' where we denote ''F''(''p'',&thinsp;''q'') by ''F''<sub>''p'',''q''</sub> for every (''p'',&thinsp;''q'') ∈ ''S'' × ''S'', the [[ordered pair]] (''S'',&thinsp;''F'') is said to be a probabilistic metric space if:
*For all ''u'' and ''v'' in ''S'', {{math|1=''u'' = ''v''}} if and only if {{math|1=''F''<sub>''u'',''v''</sub>(''x'') = 1}} for all ''x'' > 0.
*For all ''u'' and ''v'' in ''S'', {{math|1=''F''<sub>''u'',''v''</sub> = ''F''<sub>''v'',''u''</sub>}}.
*For all ''u'', ''v'' and ''w'' in ''S'', {{math|1=''F''<sub>''u'',''v''</sub>(''x'') = 1}} and {{math|1=''F''<sub>''v'',''w''</sub>(''y'') = 1 ⇒ ''F''<sub>''u'',''w''</sub>(''x'' + ''y'') = 1}} for {{math|''x'', ''y'' > 0}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Schweizer |first1=Berthold |title=Probabilistic metric spaces |last2=Sklar |first2=Abe |date=1983 |publisher=North-Holland |isbn=978-0-444-00666-0 |series=North-Holland series in probability and applied mathematics |location=New York}}</ref>

==History==
Probabilistic metric spaces are initially introduced by Menger, which were termed '''statistical metrics'''.<ref>{{Citation |author=Menger, K. | title=Selecta Mathematica | year=2003 | chapter=Statistical Metrics | pages=433–435 | publisher=Springer Vienna | doi=10.1007/978-3-7091-6045-9_35 | isbn=978-3-7091-7294-0 }}</ref> Shortly after, Wald criticized the generalized [[triangle inequality]] and proposed an alternative one.<ref>{{Citation |author=Wald, A. | year=1943 | title=On a Statistical Generalization of Metric Spaces | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=29 | issue=6 | pages=196–197 | doi=10.1073/pnas.29.6.196 | doi-access=free | pmid=16578072 | pmc=1078584 | bibcode=1943PNAS...29..196W }}</ref> However, both authors had come to the conclusion that in some respects the Wald inequality was too stringent a requirement to impose on all probability metric spaces, which is partly included in the work of Schweizer and Sklar.<ref>{{Citation |author=Schweizer, B. |author2=Sklar, A | chapter=Statistical Metrics | date=2003 | pages=433–435 | title=Selecta Mathematica | publisher=Springer Vienna | doi=10.1007/978-3-7091-6045-9_35 | isbn=978-3-7091-7294-0 }}</ref> Later, the probabilistic metric spaces found to be very suitable to be used with fuzzy sets<ref>{{cite book |author=Bede, B. | date= 2013 | title=Mathematics of Fuzzy Sets and Fuzzy Logic | series= Studies in Fuzziness and Soft Computing | volume= 295 | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | doi=10.1007/978-3-642-35221-8| isbn= 978-3-642-35220-1 }}</ref> and further called fuzzy metric spaces<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kramosil |first1=Ivan |last2=Michálek |first2=Jiří |date=1975 |title=Fuzzy metrics and statistical metric spaces |url=https://www.kybernetika.cz/content/1975/5/336/paper.pdf |journal=Kybernetika |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=336–344}}</ref>

==Probability metric of random variables==

A probability metric ''D'' between two [[random variable]]s ''X'' and ''Y'' may be defined, for example, as
<math display="block">D(X, Y) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x-y| F(x, y) \, dx \, dy</math>
where ''F''(''x'', ''y'') denotes the joint probability density function of the random variables ''X'' and ''Y''. If ''X'' and ''Y'' are independent from each other, then the equation above transforms into
<math display="block">D(X, Y) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x-y| f(x) g(y) \, dx \, dy</math>
where ''f''(''x'') and ''g''(''y'') are probability density functions of ''X'' and ''Y'' respectively.

One may easily show that such probability metrics do not satisfy the first [[metric (mathematics)|metric]] axiom or satisfies it [[If and only if|if, and only if]], both of arguments ''X'' and ''Y'' are certain events described by [[Dirac delta]] density [[Probability density function|probability distribution function]]s. In this case:
<math display="block">D(X, Y) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x-y| \delta(x-\mu_x) \delta(y-\mu_y) \, dx \, dy = |\mu_x - \mu_y|</math>
the probability metric simply transforms into the metric between [[expected value]]s <math>\mu_x</math>, <math>\mu_y</math> of the variables ''X'' and ''Y''.

For all other [[random variable]]s ''X'', ''Y'' the probability metric does not satisfy the [[identity of indiscernibles]] condition required to be satisfied by the metric of the metric space, that is:
<math display="block">D\left(X, X\right) > 0.</math>

[[Image:Probability_metric_DNN.png|thumb|right|325px|
Probability metric between two random variables ''X'' and ''Y'', both having [[normal distribution]]s and the same [[standard deviation]] <math>\sigma = 0, \sigma = 0.2, \sigma = 0.4, \sigma = 0.6, \sigma = 0.8, \sigma = 1</math> (beginning with the bottom curve).
<math>m_{xy} = |\mu_x - \mu_y|</math> denotes a distance between [[mean]]s of ''X'' and ''Y''.]]

===Example===

For example if both [[Probability density function|probability distribution function]]s of random variables ''X'' and ''Y'' are [[normal distribution]]s (N) having the same [[standard deviation]] <math>\sigma</math>, integrating <math>D\left(X, Y\right)</math> yields:
<math display="block">D_{NN}(X, Y) = \mu_{xy} + \frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt\pi} \exp\left(-\frac{\mu_{xy}^2}{4\sigma^2}\right) - \mu_{xy} \operatorname{erfc} \left(\frac{\mu_{xy}}{2\sigma}\right)</math>
where
<math display="block">\mu_{xy} = \left|\mu_x - \mu_y\right|,</math>
and <math>\operatorname{erfc}(x)</math> is the complementary [[error function]].

In this case:
<math display="block">\lim_{\mu_{xy} \to 0} D_{NN}(X, Y) = D_{NN}(X, X) = \frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt\pi}.</math>

==Probability metric of random vectors==

The probability metric of random variables may be extended into metric ''D''('''X''', '''Y''') of [[random vector]]s '''X''', '''Y''' by substituting <math>|x-y|</math> with any metric operator ''d''('''x''', '''y'''):
<math display="block">D(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}) = \int_\Omega \int_\Omega d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) F(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \, d\Omega_x d\Omega_y</math>
where ''F''('''X''', '''Y''') is the joint probability density function of random vectors '''X''' and '''Y'''. For example substituting ''d''('''x''', '''y''') with [[Euclidean metric]] and providing the vectors '''X''' and '''Y''' are mutually independent would yield to:
<math display="block">D(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}) = \int_{\Omega} \int_{\Omega} \sqrt{\sum_i |x_i - y_i|^2} F(\mathbf{x}) G(\mathbf{y}) \, d\Omega_x d\Omega_y.</math>
